questions.question: A candidate has a 0.8% aggregate violation rate, but its critical accessibility slice has a 95% upper bound above the declared limit. What is the defensible release decision?
options: Hold or restrict the affected release path until the critical slice has passing evidence.
Release because the aggregate rate is below 1%.
Remove the slice because it represents little traffic.
Average the critical result with the strongest language slice.
questions.explanation: A healthy aggregate cannot cancel a blocking high-impact slice. The team needs containment or stronger passing evidence for that declared boundary.

questions.question: Why can traffic-proportional sampling be unsafe for a low-volume, high-severity slice?
options: It may allocate too few cases to estimate the slice precisely or exercise rare failure paths.
It always produces more false positives than equal sampling.
It changes the production traffic distribution.
It prevents evaluators from returning structured labels.
questions.explanation: Production prevalence and evaluation importance are different. Rare slices often require intentional oversampling when a miss has asymmetric impact.

questions.question: A critical-harm test observes zero violations in 80 cases. What should the report conclude?
options: No violations were observed, but the sample still permits a non-zero upper rate and may be insufficient for release.
The true violation rate is exactly zero.
The evaluator has perfect recall.
The harm can be removed from production monitoring.
questions.explanation: Finite samples create uncertainty. A Wilson bound makes that uncertainty visible instead of treating zero observed failures as proof of zero risk.

questions.question: Which validation best supports using a model-based judge for multilingual safety labels?
options: Measure agreement and disagreement patterns against qualified human labels in each relevant language and harm slice.
Confirm that the judge model is larger than the system under test.
Use the same prompt for every language without review.
Accept the judge if its global average exceeds 90%.
questions.explanation: Evaluator validity is conditional on domain, language, harm, rubric, and boundary cases. Global agreement can hide concentrated grader failures.

questions.question: Why must a safety gate include benign product-utility cases?
options: A stricter mitigation can reduce one harm while causing excessive refusals or unequal access.
Utility cases make confidence intervals unnecessary.
Utility and safety always use the same threshold.
A high utility score proves the system is fair.
questions.explanation: False positives and overblocking can also harm users. Safety evidence should expose the trade-off rather than optimizing violations in isolation.

questions.question: A production incident is fixed. What makes the resulting regression suitable for a future release gate?
options: A minimized fixture, expected boundary, affected slice, severity, version identity, owner, and blocking rule.
A permanent copy of every raw user message.
A screenshot of the incident dashboard.
A one-time manual confirmation with no version record.
questions.explanation: A durable regression preserves the failure mechanism and governance identity while minimizing sensitive incident data.

questions.question: What is the strongest reason not to report one composite safety score?
options: Aggregation lets success on common or moderate harms numerically offset a failing critical harm or affected slice.
Composite scores cannot be displayed in dashboards.
Every safety metric must be qualitative.
A composite score requires more than one evaluator.
questions.explanation: Safety dimensions are not interchangeable units. Keeping severity and slices separate preserves blocking failures and their operational consequences.
